title: GraphQL Schema Design: The Type System Handbook
summary: A deep tour of the GraphQL type system — scalars, objects, enums, interfaces, unions, non-null and list wrappers — covering how the schema is defined, validated, and executed, plus nullability trade-offs, versioning pitfalls, and the mistakes that break clients.

chapters.title: The Schema Is the Contract
points: GraphQL schema = strongly typed graph of what a client may ask for; server publishes it, client queries against it
SDL (Schema Definition Language) is the canonical text form: `type`, `enum`, `interface`, `union`, `input`, `scalar`, `directive`
Three root operation types: `Query` (reads), `Mutation` (writes), `Subscription` (event streams); only `Query` is required
`schema { query: Query, mutation: Mutation }` block is optional — default root names Query/Mutation/Subscription are assumed
Every field resolves to exactly one type; there is no `any`, no untyped bag, no dynamic field set
Validation is static: a query is checked against the schema before a single resolver runs (validation phase precedes execution)
Schema is introspectable at runtime via `__schema` and `__type` — this powers GraphiQL, codegen, and client type safety
Type names are globally unique in one schema; no namespaces, so naming discipline matters (`UserAddress` not `Address` twice)
Names must match `/[_A-Za-z][_0-9A-Za-z]*/`; names beginning `__` are reserved for introspection
Descriptions use `"""triple-quoted strings"""` above the definition — these are machine-readable docs, not comments; `#` comments are dropped
Example minimal schema: `type Query { me: User }` + `type User { id: ID!, name: String! }`
Schema-first (write SDL, generate resolvers) vs code-first (write code, generate SDL) — same type system, different authoring ergonomics
The schema is the versioning surface: additive changes are safe, removals and type changes break clients
Mental model: the schema is a type graph; a query is a path selection through it that returns a tree shaped like the query

chapters.title: Scalars: The Leaves of Every Query
points: Scalars are leaf types — they resolve to a concrete value and cannot have a selection set
Five built-ins: `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Boolean`, `ID`
`Int` is signed 32-bit: range −2^31 to 2^31−1; values outside must be a custom scalar or a `String`
`Float` is IEEE-754 double precision; never use it for money — use a `Decimal` custom scalar or integer minor units
`String` is UTF-8 text; serialized as a JSON string
`ID` serializes as a String but signals "opaque identifier, do not do math on it"; accepts Int or String input and coerces to String
`ID` equality is string equality — `1` and `"1"` as input both become `"1"`
Custom scalars: `scalar DateTime` declares the name; the server supplies `serialize`, `parseValue`, `parseLiteral`
`serialize` = internal value to JSON (output); `parseValue` = variable to internal (input); `parseLiteral` = inline AST literal to internal (input)
Common custom scalars: `DateTime` (ISO-8601), `JSON`, `URL`, `EmailAddress`, `BigInt`, `UUID`
Custom scalars are validation boundaries — throw in `parseValue` and the request is rejected before any resolver runs
Cost of `scalar JSON`: it is an escape hatch that destroys type safety, introspection value, and codegen; use sparingly
Input coercion rules: `Int` accepts an int literal only; `Float` accepts int or float literals (int is widened); `String` does not silently accept numbers
Gotcha: a custom scalar's semantics live in the server code, not the SDL, so two services can define `DateTime` incompatibly — federation must align them

chapters.title: Object Types and Fields
points: `type User { ... }` defines an object type: a named set of fields, each with its own type
Field syntax: `name(arg: Type = default): ReturnType @directive`
Object types are the only types that can appear with a selection set; every query path must end at a scalar or enum
Fields can take arguments — arguments are how GraphQL expresses filtering, pagination, and formatting per field, not just per query
Argument types must be input types: scalars, enums, input objects, and their list/non-null wrappers — never an object type
Default argument values: `posts(first: Int = 10): [Post!]!`; a default makes an argument effectively optional
Resolvers have signature `(parent, args, context, info)`; the parent is the resolved value of the enclosing field
Default resolver behavior: if no resolver is given, the engine reads `parent[fieldName]` (property or method)
Fields resolve independently and lazily — a field with no resolver cost is free if the client does not select it
Sibling fields on one object resolve in parallel; a mutation's top-level fields resolve serially, left to right
`input` types are separate from `type`: `input CreateUserInput { name: String! }` — you cannot use `User` as an argument type
Why input/output split exists: outputs can have arguments and interfaces; inputs must be plain, serializable, and cycle-safe by nullability
Circular references are fine and normal: `type User { posts: [Post!]! }` and `type Post { author: User! }`
`extend type Query { ... }` splits a root type across files/modules — key to schema modularity and federation
Cost gotcha: nested object fields cause the N+1 problem; batch with DataLoader per-request rather than restructuring the schema

chapters.title: Enums: Closed Sets of Values
points: `enum Role { ADMIN EDITOR VIEWER }` defines a fixed, validated set of symbolic values
Enum values are unquoted in queries and variables are quoted strings: `role: ADMIN` inline, `"ADMIN"` as a JSON variable
Enums are a leaf type — like scalars, no selection set
Convention: `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` values; `true`, `false`, and `null` are forbidden as enum value names
Server-side an enum value can map to any internal value (`ADMIN` to `1`, or to `"admin"`) via a value map
Enums self-document in introspection, so tools render dropdowns and codegen emits union string types automatically
Enum vs String: enum gives validation, introspection, and codegen; String gives freedom to add values without a schema change
Adding an enum value is a breaking change for output positions — existing clients' exhaustive switches encounter an unknown value
Adding an enum value is safe for input positions; removing one is breaking for input, safe-ish for output
Mitigation for growth: model open sets (country codes, tags) as `String` or a custom scalar, closed sets (status, sort order) as enums
`@deprecated(reason: "...")` works on enum values as well as fields — deprecated values stay valid but disappear from default introspection
Common uses: `SortDirection { ASC DESC }`, `OrderStatus { PENDING SHIPPED CANCELLED }`, `CacheControlScope { PUBLIC PRIVATE }`
Gotcha: enums are not integers — do not rely on ordinal position, and do not renumber internal mappings casually
Gotcha: an enum used in both input and output positions inherits the breaking-change rules of both, so it evolves the slowest

chapters.title: Non-Null and Lists: The Wrapping Types
points: Two wrapping types only: Non-Null `!` and List `[]`; everything else is a named type
Wrappers compose and read inside-out: `[String!]!` is a non-null list of non-null strings
The four shapes of `[String]`: `[String]` (list nullable, items nullable), `[String!]` (list nullable, items non-null), `[String]!` (list non-null, items nullable), `[String!]!` (both non-null)
`[String]` may return `null`, `[]`, `["a", null]`; `[String!]!` may only return `[]` or `["a"]`
Non-null is a guarantee to the client: the field will never be `null` in a successful response
Null propagation (the bubbling rule): if a non-null field resolves to null or errors, the null bubbles up to the nearest nullable parent, wiping that entire subtree
If nulls bubble all the way to the root and the root field is non-null, `data` becomes `null` — one bad field can nuke the whole response
This is why `Query` root fields are usually nullable: a failing `me: User` should not erase a sibling `feed`
Inside a `[Post!]!`, one failed item nullifies the whole list; inside `[Post]!`, that item becomes `null` and the rest survives — a deliberate resilience trade-off
Errors always appear in the top-level `errors` array with a `path`, regardless of where the null landed
Nullable to non-null on an output field is a safe change (clients get a stronger guarantee); non-null to nullable is breaking
For arguments and input fields the direction inverts: non-null to nullable is safe, nullable to non-null is breaking
A non-null argument with no default must be supplied on every call; a non-null argument with a default may be omitted
Lists are not paginated by nature — `[Post!]!` invites unbounded result sets; use a Connection with `first`/`after` for anything that can grow
Design heuristic: be liberal with nullable outputs at boundaries you don't control (remote services), strict inside your own data
Gotcha: `null` and "field not requested" are different — an unrequested field is simply absent from the response object

chapters.title: Interfaces: Shared Shape, Many Implementations
points: `interface Node { id: ID! }` declares an abstract type: a field set that implementing types must provide
`type User implements Node { id: ID!, name: String! }` — the implementer must include every interface field
Querying an interface field returns any implementing type; shared fields are selectable directly without a fragment
Type-specific fields require an inline fragment: `... on User { email }` or a named fragment spread
`__typename` is the meta-field every object exposes — always request it on abstract types so clients can discriminate and normalize the cache
Servers must supply `resolveType` (or `isTypeOf` per type) so the engine knows which concrete type a value is; without it, execution errors at runtime
Implementations may add fields freely; they may not remove or narrow interface fields incompatibly
Covariant return rule: an implementing field may return a subtype or a more non-null version (`String` to `String!` is legal; `String!` to `String` is not)
Multiple interfaces per type: `type User implements Node & Actor` — ampersand-separated
Interfaces can implement other interfaces (since the 2020 spec): `interface Resource implements Node`, and it must then declare `id: ID!` too
The `Node` pattern: a global `node(id: ID!): Node` field gives every object a globally unique ID and one refetch entry point — the basis of Relay's cache
Interfaces express "is-a" with shared fields, so they are the right tool when clients want to query common fields across types uniformly
Cost: every interface field is a contract on all implementers — adding a field to a widely implemented interface is a wide-reaching change
Gotcha: an interface with no implementers is legal SDL but can never resolve to anything
Gotcha: forgetting `__typename` on an interface selection leaves normalized clients (Apollo, Relay) unable to cache the result correctly

chapters.title: Unions: One Field, Unrelated Types
points: `union SearchResult = User | Post | Comment` — a value is exactly one of the listed types
Union members must be object types: no scalars, no enums, no interfaces, no other unions, no input types
Unions declare no common fields, so every selection needs an inline fragment plus optionally `__typename`
Query shape: `search(q: $q) { __typename ... on User { name } ... on Post { title } }`
You may select `__typename` on a union without any fragment — it is the only universally available field
Like interfaces, unions require server-side `resolveType` to map a runtime value to a member type
Interface vs union: interface = shared fields, "is-a"; union = no shared fields, "one-of"
Adding a member to a union is a breaking change in practice — existing clients have no fragment for the new type and get an empty object
Defensive client pattern: always include a fallback branch and treat unknown `__typename` as a degraded render, not a crash
Errors-as-data pattern: `union CreateUserResult = CreateUserSuccess | EmailTaken | RateLimited` makes expected failures typed and non-null instead of top-level errors
Why errors-as-data helps: the `errors` array is untyped and loses non-null guarantees; a result union keeps failure modes in the schema and in codegen
A union can be combined with an interface: give all members a shared `interface Error { message: String! }` so clients can render any failure generically
Search, feeds, activity streams, and notification lists are the canonical union use cases
Gotcha: a union cannot be used as an input type — there is no input union in the spec (input polymorphism is emulated with a one-of input object)
Gotcha: unions have no field-level guarantees, so a union of many members forces long, brittle client queries — prefer an interface when types genuinely share fields

chapters.title: Validation and Execution: What the Engine Actually Does
points: Request lifecycle: parse to AST, validate against schema, coerce variables, execute, format response
Parse errors and validation errors return before execution — the response has `errors` and no `data` key at all
Key validation rules: fields must exist on the type, leaf fields must have no selection set, composite fields must have one, fragments must be on possible types
Field merging rule: two selections with the same response key must be mergeable (same field, compatible arguments) or the query is invalid
Variables are coerced against their declared types before execution; a bad variable is a request-level error, not a field error
Variable declaration must be at least as strict as the argument it fills: `$x: String` cannot feed `arg: String!` unless `$x` has a default
Execution walks the query tree depth-first through the type graph; each field's resolved value becomes the next `parent`
Non-null fields that error trigger the bubbling rule; nullable fields absorb the error and return `null` in place
`errors[].path` locates the failure exactly; `extensions` carries machine-readable codes — use them, don't parse messages
`@skip(if:)` and `@include(if:)` are the two built-in query directives — evaluated during execution, they prune the selection set
`@deprecated(reason:)` and `@specifiedBy(url:)` are the built-in schema directives; deprecated fields still execute normally
Introspection query cost: `__schema` is expensive and leaks design — commonly disabled in production alongside persisted queries
Depth and complexity limits are not in the spec — you must add query depth limiting, cost analysis, or persisted queries yourself
Aliases (`a: user(id:1)`) let one query select the same field multiple times with different arguments, and shape the response keys
Subscription execution differs: it resolves one root field to an event stream and re-executes the selection set per event

chapters.title: Evolving a Schema Without Breaking Clients
points: GraphQL's versioning story is continuous evolution: add fields, deprecate old ones, never ship /v2
Safe (additive): new type, new nullable field, new optional argument, new interface implementation, new enum value in input-only position
Breaking: removing a field or type, renaming anything, making an output field nullable, making an argument non-null, changing a field's type
`@deprecated(reason: "Use fullName")` marks a field or enum value; tooling hides it and clients see the migration hint
Deprecation is only step one — you need field-level usage analytics before you can safely delete
Changing `[Post]` to `[Post!]!` is safe for clients (stronger guarantee) but forces the server to never return item nulls
Adding a required argument breaks every existing query; add it as nullable with a default instead, then tighten later
Enum output growth is the classic silent break — clients that exhaustively switch will hit an unhandled case
Union member growth is the same trap — clients without a fallback fragment render nothing for the new member
Schema checks in CI (compare proposed SDL against the registered schema plus real traffic) are the practical guardrail
Nullability is the hardest thing to change later — decide it deliberately at design time, not by defaulting everything to non-null
Prefer input objects over long argument lists: `createUser(input: CreateUserInput!)` lets you add fields without touching the signature
Pagination as a Connection (`edges`/`node`/`pageInfo`) is future-proofing: a bare `[Post!]!` cannot gain a cursor later without a break
Naming is permanent in practice — a bad type name costs more than a bad field implementation
Federation adds a rule: shared types must agree across subgraphs, so cross-team enum and scalar definitions must be coordinated

chapters.title: Mistakes, Trade-offs, and the Cheat Sheet
points: Mistake: making everything non-null — one failing subfield then blanks a whole page via null bubbling
Mistake: making everything nullable — clients drown in defensive null checks and codegen types become useless
Rule of thumb: `id` and enum-like discriminators non-null; anything backed by a remote call or optional data nullable
Mistake: `scalar JSON` as a catch-all — kills introspection, codegen, and validation; the client is back to guessing
Mistake: exposing database columns 1:1 — the schema should model the client's domain, not your tables
Mistake: using a union where an interface fits — clients then repeat the same fields in every fragment branch
Mistake: using an interface where a union fits — you invent fake shared fields that are meaningless for half the implementers
Mistake: unbounded lists — `[Post!]!` with no `first` argument is a denial-of-service surface
Mistake: no `__typename` on abstract selections — normalized client caches silently misbehave
Mistake: passing an output type as an argument — the spec forbids it; you must define a parallel `input` type
Trade-off: enum (validated, breaks on growth) vs String (free to grow, no validation) — decide by whether the set is closed
Trade-off: errors in the `errors` array (simple, untyped) vs result unions (typed, verbose) — use unions for expected domain failures, `errors` for bugs and infrastructure
Trade-off: deep nesting (expressive, N+1-prone) vs flatter types (cheaper, less graph-like) — solve with DataLoader, not schema flattening
Cheat sheet — abstract types: interface = shared fields + is-a; union = no shared fields + one-of; both need `resolveType` and `__typename`
Cheat sheet — wrappers: `T` nullable, `T!` guaranteed, `[T]` nullable list of nullables, `[T!]!` guaranteed list of guaranteed items
Cheat sheet — change safety: output nullable to non-null safe, non-null to nullable breaking; input non-null to nullable safe, nullable to non-null breaking
